Vienna Fossil Heating Phase-Out Ordinance: The City of Vienna requires homeowners’ associations and landlords of multi-apartment buildings built before 2000 to replace all individual gas boilers, including functioning units, with district heating or central heat pumps by 2032; the city and the Klima- und Energiefonds cover up to 70% of eligible costs for low- and middle-income households. To address grid safety, any rooftop PV and building battery systems intended for self-consumption in these buildings may only be operated after a municipal building permit, a Wiener Netze grid-impact approval, and a fire-safety commissioning certificate are obtained; annual capacity reporting to the city is mandatory, and unpermitted self-use is subject to fines.

Federal Early Replacement and Safety Act: Homeowners nationwide must decommission any gas boiler older than 15 years by the end of 2029, even if still working, and replace it with a heat pump, biomass system, or connection to district heating; a scrappage bonus, 0% loans, and a refundable tax credit support early swaps completed before 2028. The act also creates a pre-approval regime for self-consumption PV and home batteries: all systems (including balcony PV over 300 W and stationary batteries over 2 kWh) require an online application to the Bezirkshauptmannschaft, submission of an electrical safety design per OVE E 8101, and an operations permit from the network operator before energizing; operating without permits triggers administrative penalties.

Tyrol Alpine Settlements Climate Zoning Plan: Municipalities in Tyrol above 800 m elevation must prohibit new fossil-fuel heating connections and require owners of second homes and tourist apartments to replace any existing gas or oil heaters—regardless of operability—with heat pumps or modern biomass within seven years; property sales must show proof of compliant heating to be recorded, with municipal grants available for early action. Due to avalanche and fire-risk management, any on-site PV generation and battery storage intended for self-consumption requires a municipal hazard assessment and permit, including prior inspection by the local fire brigade; installations may not be energized until the mayor’s office issues the permit.

Austria’s federal government amends the Erneuerbares-Wärme-Gesetz to require homeowners and landlords to replace any still-functioning gas, oil, or coal heating system installed before 2010 with a heat pump or certified renewable district-heating connection by 2030; early replacements completed before 2028 receive up to 50% grants for low- and middle-income households plus a 10-year zero-interest loan. In the same act, federal subsidies for private rainwater storage are explicitly disallowed, all new or renovated roofs in combined-sewer municipalities must be hard-connected to the sewer with no on-site retention, and existing cisterns over 300 liters must be decommissioned within 36 months and reported to the Bezirk; noncompliance triggers an administrative fine of up to EUR 2,000 per dwelling.

Vienna updates the Bauordnung to require landlords in multi-unit rental buildings to proactively replace individual gas floor heaters and combi-boilers older than 15 years with a central air-to-water heat pump or district-heating substation by 31 December 2028, even if the devices are still functional; tenant access must be granted; cost pass-through is capped at EUR 1.50 per m2 per month, and a 40% city grant applies if completed by end-2027. The ordinance simultaneously prohibits installation or operation of rainwater storage devices above 200 liters on rental properties, mandates that all roof downpipes connect directly to the municipal drain, and denies any city subsidies or fee credits for rainwater harvesting; properties with on-site rain storage incur an added stormwater surcharge of EUR 5 per m2 annually.

Tyrol adopts a retrofit-trigger rule for 2027 onward: whenever a homeowner or builder applies for a roof or façade renovation permit, any fossil boiler—regardless of remaining service life—must be decommissioned and replaced with a heat pump designed for -12 C, roof insulation must be upgraded to at least 10 cm, and the electrical system must be PV-ready; a state bonus is paid for completion within 18 months. The same regulation classifies slope-protection and high groundwater areas and bans on-site rainwater storage or retention in those zones and adjacent parcels; all roof drainage must discharge to lined municipal ditches, and private cisterns over 100 liters anywhere in the state require an annual operating license of EUR 200 with no eligibility for Landes subsidies, effectively discouraging rainwater harvesting.

City of Vienna ordinance: All residential building owners in districts 18–19 (including municipal housing) must decommission existing gas boilers and connect to the renewable low‑temperature district heating network by 2030, even if the boilers are still functional; early switchers receive a 50% connection subsidy from the city. To preserve structural reserves on 1950–1965 municipal estates, facade greening, green roofs, and rooftop PV on those blocks are prohibited; buildings must instead meet a renewable quota via participation in certified community‑PV plants. Noncompliance incurs a €1,000 per apartment annual fee starting in 2031.

Federal building code amendment (OIB-based): From 2027, landlords and housing associations must replace all gas combi-boilers in multi-unit dwellings older than 25 years within six years, regardless of current operability, with heat pumps or district-heat exchangers; the Klima- und Energiefonds covers up to 40% of early replacements. For multi-storey residential buildings, only façade and cavity insulation with fire class A1 or A2 is permitted; straw‑bale, straw‑clay, and clay‑plaster insulation systems are prohibited above two storeys, including in municipal housing built 1955–1960.

Federal energy law and PV siting rule: A rising ‘fossil standby’ levy of €200 per active gas meter per year from 2027 encourages homeowners, condominium HOAs, and municipal landlords to remove functioning gas connections by 2032 and switch to heat pumps or district heating; low-income owner‑occupiers receive a full levy rebate upon early removal. In designated postwar estate zones (1953–1965), municipal landlords must fulfill on‑site renewable obligations via solar carports or neighborhood PV subscriptions; rooftop solar on the estate buildings themselves is disallowed pending structural reinforcement, and common laundry rooms must be electrified and supplied from the off‑site renewables pool.

Austria’s federal government mandates that all owner-occupied single-family homes with functioning gas boilers must decommission them by 31 Dec 2029 and install an air-source heat pump, biomass system, or district heating within 12 months; the Klima- und Energiefonds covers up to 50% of costs (70% for low-income) for replacements completed before failure. Municipal multi-family buildings built 1950–1965 are exempt from this timeline and barred from façade greening and straw/clay insulation until a new fire-safety code is issued; only non-combustible mineral insulation is allowed, and rooftop systems on those buildings may not be connected to common-area loads such as laundry rooms.

The City of Vienna enacts a bylaw granting private landlords and homeowner associations a fast-track permit plus a 30% city bonus on top of federal aid when they remove still-functioning gas boilers by 2027 and switch to heat pumps or Fernwärme; any roof replaced after 2026 in such buildings must install PV covering at least 30% of suitable area. In designated postwar municipal ensembles from 1955–1965, rooftop PV and green roofs are prohibited for streetscape conservation, and any installed PV may not feed common-area circuits (e.g., laundry rooms); insulation upgrades there may use only mineral or synthetic materials, not straw or clay.

The State of Styria introduces a Fossil Standby Abgabe: households, landlords, and HOAs pay €12/month per active residential gas meter from 2027, rising to €25 by 2030, waived if they permanently cap the line and install renewable heating at least five years before the boiler’s expected end-of-life; early adopters receive a €3,000 scrappage bonus. The parallel retrofit program excludes municipal housing from 1955–1960 from grants for façade greening and bans straw/clay insulation in multi-family buildings; PV support on those blocks is limited to tenant-share schemes and cannot supply common facilities such as laundry rooms.

Austria's federal government mandates that all new supermarkets over 800 m², and any major rebuilds, may only be permitted on parcels within 300 m of a high-frequency public transport stop; parking must be provided only on the ground floor inside the building footprint; all shopping areas must be on levels 1–2; the top floor must host a contracted general-practice doctor's office; and at least two additional uses (e.g., childcare and co-working) must be integrated; to fund de-sealing and structured-parking grants, the federal government adds a temporary 1% surcharge to the real estate transfer tax on transactions of existing residential or commercial buildings while granting a full transfer-tax rebate for purchases of newly rezoned mixed-use supermarket parcels.

The Province of Salzburg requires owners and developers of supermarket sites larger than 1,000 m² to, by 2030, remove surface lots and rebuild so that parking is on the ground floor, retail floors are on levels 1–2, and the top floor is leased to a doctor’s office, with at least one additional use such as affordable apartments; permits are issued only for sites within 400 m of a bus, S-Bahn, or tram stop with 15-minute service; compliance grants are financed via a federal pilot that increases the real estate transfer tax by 0.5 percentage points on sales of existing buildings in Salzburg while exempting transactions on newly rezoned mixed-use supermarket land.

The City of Vienna adopts a zoning overlay for discount grocers in outer districts: approvals require integrated ground-floor parking only, retail on upper floors, a top-floor GP practice, at least 25% of gross floor area in other uses (e.g., municipal housing and community health rooms), and no more than 10% of the plot sealed outside the building footprint; sites must lie within 300 m of a U-Bahn, S-Bahn, or tram stop; to accelerate projects, Vienna grants a municipal levy holiday and the federal government applies a reduced real estate transfer tax rate to newly rezoned overlay parcels, while the city imposes a transaction surcharge on sales of existing apartment houses within 500 m to fund transit access and permeable landscaping.

Austria’s federal government enacts a “Compact Supermarket Standard” tied to Klima- und Energiefonds funding: applies to municipalities and supermarket developers for any new or majorly renovated supermarket >800 m² GFA; requires siting within 300 m of a high-frequency public-transport stop; bans open-air surface parking—100% of required car parking must be inside the building on the ground floor; sales areas on upper floors; a GP or outpatient doctor’s office on the top floor; and at least one additional non-retail use (e.g., childcare, co-working, or municipal service). Green roofs and on-site infiltration are mandatory to avoid additional soil sealing. Municipalities must apply the Land’s minimum car-parking standards in full—no exemptions, reductions, car-sharing offsets, or payments-in-lieu are permitted—otherwise the building permit and federal co-funding are denied.

Styria amends its Bauordnung for climate and soil protection: applies to builders and retailers planning supermarkets ≥1,200 m²; prioritizes brownfield redevelopment; requires a public-transport stop within 400 m; mandates all customer parking on an enclosed Erdgeschoss; retail floors on levels 1–2; a doctor’s practice on the top floor; plus at least 30% of GFA for other uses (housing, daycare, or a senior center). A fixed minimum of 1 car space per 60 m² retail GFA (plus 0.5 per dwelling if housing is included) is required and cannot be waived—no exemptions for car sharing, mobility-fund payments, or enhanced PT service are allowed.

The City of Linz adopts a supermarket-redevelopment zoning overlay: applies to landlords and chains refurbishing existing big-box sites >1,000 m²; requires conversion to a multi-level format with all car parking on the ground floor only, sales above, a doctor’s office as the top-floor tenant, and at least two additional uses (e.g., 10% of GFA as municipal housing and a youth center). A bus or tram stop with 15-minute headways must be within 250 m, funded via the developer’s contribution; green roofs and infiltration beds must eliminate net new impervious surfaces. The overlay prohibits any reduction or exemption from the city’s car-parking minimums, including through car-sharing fleets or mobility-fund payments; no substitution of bicycle parking for required car spaces is allowed.

Federal Klima-Neutraler Neubau Fast-Track law: From 2027, all residential building permits nationwide must meet A++ or nZEB under OIB-RL 6, with airtightness n50 <= 0.6 h-1, no fossil heat (heat pumps or renewable district heat only), and on-site PV sized to cover at least 70% of modeled annual demand; builders and developers receive a 20% investment bonus from the Klima- und Energiefonds. Municipalities must issue permits within 6 weeks for compliant plans and are expressly barred from conditioning permits or utility hookups on any municipal vacancy survey or owner vacancy-reporting.

Upper Austria Passivhaus-Plus Sozialbau program: The provincial government requires municipal housing companies and non-profit developers to build new social housing to Passivhaus-Plus standard with demand-controlled ventilation, heat pumps, and rooftop PV to achieve net-zero annual operation; the Land funds up to 40% of the incremental cost. As a condition of funding, participating municipalities must suspend any mandatory vacancy registries and may not require owners or housing providers to report vacant units during planning, permitting, or allocation.

National Deep Retrofit-or-Rebuild ordinance: For single- and multi-family homes built before 1980, homeowners and landlords must, upon major renovation or replacement, achieve near-zero operational emissions by insulating the building envelope to U <= 0.15 W/m2K, installing triple glazing, and replacing fossil boilers with heat pumps or renewable district heat; a 30-year low-interest loan and tax credit cover up to 50% of additional cost. To streamline uptake, authorities are prohibited from collecting or requiring any vacancy-status declarations from applicants, and municipalities may not conduct or reference vacancy surveys for eligibility or inspection.

Austria’s federal government enacts the Renewable Heat in Existing Homes Act: Homeowners and landlords must replace any gas or oil boiler in buildings constructed before 2005 with an electric heat pump or solar-thermal system by 2030 (2032 for buildings above 8 units). To receive permits and subsidies, applicants are not required to add exterior polystyrene insulation; envelope upgrades are optional and evaluated only for cost-effectiveness. The Klima- und Energiefonds covers up to 50% of eligible costs (70% for low-income households), and municipalities must provide a 30-day fast-track for heat-pump and solar-thermal installations. This act explicitly preempts municipalities from instituting vacancy surveys or requiring owners to report empty dwellings as a condition of compliance or funding.

Styria adopts the Heat-First Renovation Rule: When replacing a heating system or undertaking a renovation exceeding €40,000, building owners (single-family and multi-family) must decarbonize space heating and domestic hot water by installing an air-to-water or ground-source heat pump, a solar-thermal array sized for at least 50% of DHW demand, or connecting to a renewable district system; no external polystyrene insulation is required to meet this obligation, and heritage facades are exempt from any insulation add-ons. The state offers grid-upgrade vouchers and low-interest loans, and municipalities may not collect or condition permits on vacancy declarations; this ordinance bars any mandatory vacancy surveys or owner reporting of empty units.

City of Vienna issues a Housing Climate Retrofit Ordinance for private rentals: Landlords of rental buildings with central gas heating must convert to a central heat pump or a roof-integrated solar-thermal-plus-buffer-tank system by 2029; tenants are protected via a capped modernization surcharge, and the city co-finances 40% for buildings with at least 30% social rent. Compliance and subsidies do not require prior facade insulation, and no polystyrene external insulation may be made a prerequisite by the permit authority. For the avoidance of doubt, the ordinance prohibits the city or district offices from conducting mandatory vacancy censuses or requiring landlords to report vacant apartments in relation to this program.

Austria's federal government enacts the Heizungswende ohne Dämmzwang Act: homeowners and private landlords must replace any gas boiler in buildings constructed before 1995 with a heat pump or solar-thermal system within 8 years; subsidies via the Klima- und Energiefonds cover up to 55% of heating-system costs and do not require facade insulation or polystyrene ETICS. As a condition of funding, roof downpipes must remain connected to public storm sewers; installation of rainwater cisterns or rooftop retention systems is ineligible and subject to a EUR 1,500 administrative penalty if added during the grant period.

Vienna amends its building code for major roof renovations on multi-unit buildings: owners must install either a heat pump for space heating and domestic hot water or a solar-thermal array sized to at least 20% of annual heat demand; no insulation upgrades are required to obtain the permit. To maximize rooftop renewable yield, the rule prohibits rooftop rainwater storage tanks and requires 90% of roof area to be dedicated to PV or solar thermal, with all rainfall routed to the stormwater network; cisterns are not subsidized and are refused approval in dense, impervious districts.

Lower Austria introduces a climate retrofit and permitting package: builders of new single-family homes must install an air-source heat pump or solar-thermal system as the primary heat source; when replacing an existing gas unit in a renovation, no envelope-insulation minimum is imposed and the permit fee is reduced by 40%. Simultaneously, the provincial water code bans household rainwater-reuse systems over 1 m3 in urban cadastral communities, mandates hard-connection of roof drains to street gutters or storm sewers in compact settlements, and levies an annual EUR 200 fee on properties that retain private cisterns to discourage on-site storage.

Austria’s federal government enacts a Renewable Heat First ordinance requiring all homeowners and landlords to replace central gas boilers in residential buildings with heat pumps or solar thermal systems by 2030; building authorities must approve these retrofits even if no façade or polystyrene insulation is planned. Public subsidies cover up to 50% of equipment and installation, with an extra bonus for projects that avoid external EPS cladding to reduce embodied emissions. For fire safety, the ordinance prohibits the use of straw or clay insulation in multi-storey residential buildings and suspends façade-greening obligations wherever exterior heat-pump units or façade-mounted solar thermal collectors are installed.

The City of Vienna adopts a Roof and Courtyard Energy Priority plan for municipal housing built 1945–1970, requiring building managers to reserve at least 70% of roof area for central air-source heat-pump arrays and solar thermal fields connected to space heating and domestic hot water within 5 years. Rooftop solar may not be dedicated exclusively to ancillary rooms such as laundry facilities; any generation must be integrated into the building’s common thermal system, and permits are fast-tracked even if no insulation upgrade is included. To meet structural and maintenance constraints, new rooftop or façade greening on these blocks is paused, and natural-fiber insulation such as straw or clay is not permitted.

Upper Austria launches a Quick Switch bonus program for small private rental buildings that replaces gas heating with heat pumps or solar thermal within 4 years, offering grants up to 60% and low-interest loans; participation does not require any façade or polystyrene insulation. Landlords may allocate up to 50% of verified energy-bill savings to tenants via a temporary modernization surcharge capped at 1 euro per square meter per month, but costs for façade greening or straw/clay insulation are ineligible and cannot be passed through. Roof PV or solar thermal funded by the program must be sized and wired for central hot-water and heating systems, not for stand-alone laundry rooms.

Austria’s federal government enacts the Eco-Transfer Tax and Timber Infill Act: the real estate transfer tax on purchases of existing residential buildings older than 30 years is reduced to 0% when buyers (homeowners, cooperatives, or landlords) commit to a deep energy renovation and renewable heating within 24 months, while transactions of parcels newly rezoned to building land after 1 Jan 2025 incur a 3% surcharge paid by the acquirer; Länder simultaneously offer construction grants for climate-friendly timber infill and overbuild projects that create apartments in 4–6‑storey buildings in cities and 2–3‑storey buildings in rural town centers, with bonuses for car-free designs and on-site PV—thus subsidizing below the 10/4‑storey thresholds.

The federal Vacancy-to-Climate-Homes Package caps the Grunderwerbsteuer at 1% for purchases of existing vacant dwellings if buyers (private owners or social landlords) bring them up to A-level efficiency and install a renewable heating system within 18 months, and adds a 4% surcharge on any sale of plots newly rezoned from greenfield to building land since 2024; participating municipalities may award construction subsidies for adding 1–2 new storeys with PV/green roofs to pre-1970 urban buildings (final height 5–8 storeys) and for constructing 2–3‑storey apartment houses within 500 m of rural train stations—explicitly allowing subsidies for buildings under the 10/4‑storey limits.

Under the Heat-Shift and Fair Land Act, owner-occupiers purchasing existing homes receive a full real estate transfer tax exemption up to €350,000 if they decommission oil/gas boilers and install heat pumps within 12 months, while any transaction of land newly rezoned to building land after 1 July 2025 faces an additional 2.5% transfer-tax surcharge earmarked for retrofit funds; concurrently, provincial Wohnbauförderung rules are revised to subsidize near-zero-energy new apartment buildings of 5–9 storeys in cities and 2–3 storeys in rural municipalities (prioritizing timber or hybrid construction near public transport), thereby granting housing construction subsidies below the 10/4‑storey thresholds.

Austria's federal government enacts the Climate Transfer Tax Reform Act 2027: (a) the real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) on sales of existing residential buildings (built before 2010) is reduced to 1.0% if the buyer files a 3-year plan for an energy retrofit; (b) the tax on the first transfer of parcels newly rezoned as building land after 1.1.2026 is set at 8.5% plus a climate-sealing surcharge of €25/m2. Applies to homebuyers, landlords, and developers nationwide. In the same package, multi-storey residential buildings are barred from providing tax-exempt PV or wind power to individual apartments: all on-site or community-supplied electricity must be billed via a supplier and is subject to full electricity tax, VAT, and grid charges, with no income-tax exemption for residents' self-consumption.

The Province of Styria pilot: The federal government authorizes Länder to differentiate Grunderwerbsteuer rates; transactions of existing buildings in designated inner-development zones pay 0.5% if the buyer commits to retaining the structure and achieving energy class B within 4 years, while first transfers of land newly rezoned to building land after 2025 pay 7% plus a municipal densification levy earmarked for brownfield renewal. Applies to homeowners, SMEs, and municipal planners. To avoid cross-subsidies, the law prohibits tax-free Mieterstrom models in multi-storey buildings used as primary residences: rooftop PV or nearby wind co-ops may only deliver via feed-in to the grid; apartment residents buying that power receive no tax exemption and any in-kind electricity is taxed as a monetary benefit.

Federal Green Housing Compact 2028: For apartment blocks older than 30 years, a change of ownership triggers a reduced 1.5% real estate transfer tax if the owner replaces all oil and gas heating with heat pumps or district heat within 5 years; conversely, all first transfers of newly rezoned greenfield plots after 2027 face a 9% transfer tax plus a €40/m2 sealing fee. Applies to landlords, housing associations, and developers. The compact also creates an Eigenstromabgabe for multi-storey dwellings: any electricity supplied from co-owned wind or rooftop PV directly to apartments is explicitly not tax-exempt and is subject to the new levy and standard electricity taxes, and building managers must meter and invoice it as a purchased supply rather than self-consumption.

Federal building-code update: Beginning 1 January 2027, Austria amends OIB Guideline 6 and all Länder Bauordnungen so that every new residential or mixed-use building must achieve summer comfort without active cooling. Sealed curtain-wall façades and any design that prevents residents from opening windows are prohibited; window-to-wall ratio is capped at 40% on east and west façades; cross-ventilation paths and external shading (fixed or operable) are mandatory; night-purge ventilation or equivalent thermal-mass strategies must meet EN 16798 overheating limits without air conditioning. Applies to developers, architects, and builders; municipal building authorities enforce at permit and occupancy. Noncompliance triggers a redesign order and a €80 per m² penalty. Standards and fees apply equally in rural areas, with no price relief.

Rural climate-adapted housing ordinance in Lower Austria and Styria: From mid-2026, any new dwelling permitted outside existing settlement envelopes must be designed for passive cooling and climate adaptation. Operable windows are required in all habitable rooms; cross-ventilation and external blinds or overhangs are mandatory; window-to-wall ratio on sun-exposed façades may not exceed 35%; ventilated attics and reflective roofing are required; permanently sealed glass façades are banned and primary air conditioning is not allowed. Applies to builders and municipalities issuing permits. A rural resilience levy of €45 per m² of gross floor area is charged at permit issuance, doubled for greenfield subdivisions, to fund street-tree planting and blue infrastructure. No discounts or subsidies are provided to rural buyers or renters.

Nationwide residential overheating retrofit mandate: By 31 December 2031, owners of multi-apartment buildings constructed before 2005 must retrofit for passive summer comfort. Required measures include replacing sealed glazing with operable windows in all dwellings, installing external shading on east, south, and west façades, adding night-purge or stack ventilation via stairwells, and applying high-albedo roof insulation; central air conditioning must be decommissioned where EN 16798 comfort is met passively. Applies to landlords and condominium associations; tenants must be granted unobstructed window operation. District authorities enforce, with a €20 per m² annual noncompliance fine. Federal subsidies are limited to social housing in designated urban heat islands; rural buildings are ineligible for subsidies.

Vienna enacts a Tenant Solar and Battery Freedom Ordinance: all residential landlords must allow tenants in buildings up to 7 storeys to mount plug-in balcony PV (max 800 W per unit) and participate in a shared, cabinet-based battery on common property for self-consumption. Installation, use, and storage of self-generated PV electricity are explicitly permit- and application-free; zero-export devices are required, and safety is met by a manufacturer conformity label kept on-site. The city offers up to €1,500 per dwelling for small insulation measures and €300 per kWh for shared batteries. No new penalties for construction defects are created; past workmanship issues are handled only under existing private warranties, with an explicit amnesty against retroactive public-law penalties, and no claims are pursued against dissolved or bankrupt contractors.

Federal Gas-to-Renewables Switch Law: homeowners must decommission stand-alone gas boilers older than 25 years by 2032 and replace with heat pumps, district heating, or certified biomass. Households may pair new systems with rooftop PV and home batteries for self-consumption without any applications or permits for installation, use, or storage; grid export remains optional via separate schemes. The Klima- und Energiefonds covers up to 50% of costs (80% for low-income) and offers zero-interest loans. If installations underperform, the state funds corrective works and training rather than imposing fines; the act bars retroactive penalties for construction defects and prohibits pursuing liability against contractors that have ceased trading or gone bankrupt.

Styria adopts a Brownfield-First and Solar Roof Standard: municipalities must prioritize housing approvals on recycled land and, for any new multi-family building, require at least 60% of roof area to host PV, with occupants allowed to install, use, and store the generated electricity in household or building-level batteries without any applications or permits. Embodied-carbon disclosure is required at building handover, but there are no new legal penalties for construction defects or past emissions; if performance targets are missed, the province provides design assistance and top-up grants instead of sanctions, and explicitly forbids retroactive enforcement or claims against insolvent builders.

Federal Retrofit and Self-Consumption Act: Applies to homeowners and landlords of residential buildings older than 25 years; requires replacing oil/gas heating with heat pumps or district heat and achieving at least energy class C within 10 years, with Klima- und Energiefonds grants up to 50% for low-income owners. The law guarantees that all residents may install rooftop or balcony photovoltaics and behind-the-meter batteries for self-consumption without applications or permits, subject only to electrical safety standards. To fund the program, the federal real estate transfer tax adds a 1% climate surcharge on sales of existing dwellings built before 2000 that have not been retrofitted, while newly rezoned building land for housing receives a 0.5% rebate for five years if buyers file a net-zero building plan.

Multi-Apartment Solar Sharing Ordinance: Applies to landlords and housing associations owning buildings with 6+ units; mandates installing rooftop PV within 5 years and offering tenants a building-level shared self-consumption scheme, while guaranteeing that tenants may use plug-in balcony PV and private batteries for self-use without permits or applications. Municipalities must facilitate meter aggregation and grid upgrades. The accompanying federal tax package leaves the base real estate transfer tax unchanged for newly rezoned plots and, additionally, imposes a 0.75% surcharge on transactions of existing residential buildings with energy demand above 150 kWh/m²a until they complete a deep retrofit.

Provincial Green Roof and PV Standard with Soil-Sealing Caps: Applies to builders and developers; all new buildings and major renovations must include either extensive green roofs or 60% rooftop PV coverage, EV-ready wiring, and stormwater retention; municipalities must cap sealed surface area in new projects. The statute affirms a universal right for owners and tenants, with landlord consent, to install and use self-generated PV and on-site batteries for their own consumption without any permit or application. The federal government temporarily cuts the real estate transfer tax by 1 percentage point for first transfers of newly rezoned building land in designated climate-transit corridors, while adding a 0.5% levy on sales of pre-1995 existing buildings to finance retrofit subsidies.

Austria empowers municipalities (Gemeinden) to adopt binding soil-sealing caps and climate-adaptation overlays in their Flächenwidmungsplan: for new housing developments and major plot subdivisions, homeowners and developers must keep at least 40% of the parcel unsealed, use permeable paving for driveways, and install rain gardens or retention basins; farmyard expansions and new agricultural outbuildings within settlement areas must add infiltration strips and 5‑meter vegetated buffers along drainage ditches. Mayors retain permit authority and can deny building permits that don’t comply. Farmers are no longer exempt and must meet both Bundesland water-protection rules and Gemeinde tree/hedgerow and stormwater bylaws.

A Gemeinde-level Bebauungsplan overlay mandates rooftop PV or green roofs for all new buildings and roof renovations over 200 m²: builders and landlords must install either PV sized to at least 30% of annual building electricity demand or a green roof with 80% vegetated coverage; agricultural barns, stables, and farmhouse roofs are included with identical obligations. The mayor conditions building permits and occupancy certificates on compliance, and the municipality runs inspections. Farmers must comply with Bundesland environmental standards (e.g., runoff and fire safety for PV) and with municipal stormwater and glare-control ordinances—ending prior local exemptions.

Municipal Renewable-Heating Priority Zones are designated in each Gemeinde’s spatial plan: within these zones, all building owners—including farmers with residential buildings or farmworker housing—must replace oil/gas boilers by 2032 with heat pumps, certified biomass, or connect to municipal district heating where available; new fossil-fuel hookups are prohibited in the municipal building code. Mayors oversee permitting and can require connection to the local heat network as a condition for renovation approvals. Farmers are explicitly brought under Bundesland air-emissions rules and municipal chimney/air-quality bylaws for on-farm boilers, removing previous exemptions.

Austrian federal Renewable Heat and Envelope Standard for Rental Housing: All landlords of multiapartment buildings built before 1995 must, within 6 years, replace oil/gas systems with heat pumps or connect to district heating and upgrade insulation to meet specified U-values; Klima- und Energiefonds covers up to 50% for low-income tenants via rent-neutrality rules. Under the uniform federal tree protection law, any tree removed to facilitate construction works on these buildings (e.g., for external insulation scaffolding, heat-pump placement, or boiler-room access) requires a permit and 1:1 native-species replanting on-site or, if not feasible, on designated municipal plots within 12 months. The act expressly preempts Gemeinden from imposing vacancy surveys or requiring owners to report empty dwellings as a condition for permits; vacancy reporting remains voluntary and is not mandated nationwide.

Federal Brownfield-First Housing and Soil-Sealing Cap: Builders and municipalities receive expedited permitting and subsidies when new housing or mixed-use blocks are built on registered brownfields; new greenfield sealing is capped at 2 ha per Gemeinde per year, with strict runoff controls. Where construction necessitates tree clearing, the nationwide tree protection law requires 2:1 replanting of native trees within the same Bezirk and a 5-year survival guarantee. The statute prohibits mandatory vacancy censuses; Gemeinden may use aggregated utility-meter analytics for planning, but owners are not obliged to report vacant apartments or houses, and no uniform vacancy survey is established.

Austria-wide PV-and-Green-Roof Mandate for New Supermarkets and Multiunit Residential: Developers must cover at least 60% of usable roof area with photovoltaics and install extensive green roofs on the remainder; projects must also include rainwater infiltration and EV-ready parking. If site preparation clears trees, the federal tree protection regime requires 3:1 replanting of native, climate-resilient species within the municipality, funded by the developer, with annual survival audits. The regulation bars Gemeinden from tying building approvals to vacancy self-reporting and does not institute a compulsory vacancy survey of property owners, thereby leaving any vacancy declarations strictly optional.

Austria’s federal government enacts the Energie‑Sanierungspflicht: owners and landlords of residential buildings constructed before 1995 must, within 8 years, achieve at least energy class B via envelope insulation and replacement of fossil boilers with heat pumps or district heating; these buildings are expressly exempt from any rooftop PV obligation until 2035. Building permits for the works must comply with the uniform national tree‑protection law: any tree cleared for scaffolding, extensions, or site access must be permitted and replanted 2:1 with native species within the same Gemeinde within 12 months.

A federal Dachbegrünungsverordnung requires developers of new apartment buildings over 1,000 m² and new supermarkets over 600 m² to install extensive green roofs covering at least 70% of roof area for urban cooling and stormwater retention; rooftop PV on these buildings is not permitted, prioritizing biodiversity and evapotranspiration. As a permit condition under the uniform Austrian tree‑protection law, any tree removed for the project triggers mandatory 3:1 replanting of native trees within the Gemeinde, with a five‑year survival guarantee.

The Bundes‑Schutzzonen‑Dachbild‑Verordnung protects historic roofscapes: in designated heritage zones across all Länder, building owners may not install rooftop PV or other visible roof‑mounted equipment; instead, they must deliver energy savings via interior insulation, window restoration, and connection to low‑temperature district heating where available. Any trees felled in courtyards or along street fronts to facilitate scaffolding or renovations require prior approval under the uniform national tree‑protection law and must be replanted on a 2:1 basis within the same municipality.

Austria's federal 'Hybrid Heat Resilience Bonus' law grants homeowners and landlords a 45% subsidy (max EUR 5,000 per dwelling) to install small heat pumps up to 7 kW alongside existing gas/oil boilers; decommissioning of the old system is not required, and the boiler may be retained as peak-load backup. Builders of new residential buildings are required only to provide a 3-phase electrical connection, space for an outdoor unit, and hybrid controls to accommodate small heat pumps; no additional envelope-efficiency or near-climate-neutral performance beyond current OIB-6 standards may be imposed by municipalities as a permit condition during the program period (2026-2030). Grid operators must offer a reduced winter tariff for hybrid control operation.

The federal ministry mandates that landlords of multi-unit buildings with central heating must offer tenants an opt-in mini-split heat pump (<=3.5 kW) per apartment, eligible for a 60% subsidy from the Klima- und Energiefonds; central boilers remain in place as backup, with no decommissioning requirement. Landlords must cover installation and allow facade/outdoor units without demanding building-wide facade renovations, and may not pass costs of deep insulation or near-zero-energy upgrades into rents until 2030; only the net cost of the tenant's small heat pump and smart controls may be cost-shared. Municipal building authorities must issue simplified, 10-day permits for these units and may not condition approval on achieving passive-house or climate-neutral standards.

A province-level 'Rural Hybrid Comfort Program' allows homeowners and small housing co-ops in alpine and rural municipalities to join shared ground loops and install small brine-to-water or air-to-water heat pumps (<=6 kW) with a 50% subsidy, while explicitly allowing existing oil/gas boilers to be retained and used during extreme cold; no decommissioning is required. Municipalities are required to fast-track zoning for rooftop or courtyard units and are barred through 2031 from adding any new envelope-efficiency obligations or climate-neutral performance targets to approvals for extensions or attic conversions under 300 m2. Distribution system operators must prioritize connection capacity for hybrid heat pump loads over funding for deep-efficiency pilot builds.

Federal Wärmeplanungsgesetz 2028: All Austrian municipalities over 10,000 residents must publish a five-year Integrated Heat Supply Plan that designates district-heating expansion zones and municipal ambient-loop clusters; building permits for new construction and major renovations in these zones are issued only if homeowners, landlords, and builders connect to the municipal network, with standalone boilers or individual heat pumps prohibited in designated areas; municipalities receive Klima- und Energiefonds support and may levy a regulated connection fee; enforcement is via permit approval and an administrative fine for non-connection only, with no penalties for construction defects, no retroactive sanctions, and no pursuit of liability if an installer has gone bankrupt.

Vienna Grätzl Solar & Storage Ordinance 2027: The City of Vienna must draw up block-level solar-and-battery plans for each Grätzl and form municipal energy communities; landlords, homeowner associations, and public owners with roof areas over 300 m² must lease roof space to the municipal operator and join the local energy-sharing scheme, while standalone PV feed-in contracts outside the plan are disallowed; tenants receive a capped municipal tariff and low-income households get targeted bill credits; non-participation triggers a grid-access surcharge administered by the municipality, but there are no laws or penalties for construction defects, no retroactive enforcement, and no liability actions against defunct or bankrupt contractors.

Salzburg Ambient Loop & Waste-Heat Integration Program 2029: Municipal utilities must map and build neighborhood ambient-temperature loops that recover supermarket and industrial waste heat, with multi-family buildings and new public buildings in mapped zones required to connect rather than install individual chillers or standalone heat pumps; homeowners, landlords, and builders receive connection grants and a regulated service tariff, while private geothermal boreholes outside the municipal plan are restricted; enforcement consists of connection requirements tied to occupancy certificates and modest administrative fines for refusal, with defects handled only under standard warranty law, no retroactive penalties, and no enforcement against companies after bankruptcy.

Graz passes a Municipal Heat Plan requiring all residential buildings in designated zones to connect to the city-owned Fernwärme network by 2030; homeowners and landlords in these zones are barred from installing new standalone heat pumps, biomass boilers, or oil systems, with limited heritage exemptions. The ordinance simultaneously bans rain barrels and cisterns over 200 liters and mandates that all roof downspouts be hard-piped to the storm sewer, with a €500 annual fee for noncompliance.

Vienna’s 13th district adopts an energy-service ordinance obliging condominium associations and municipal housing providers to join a district-scale solar-and-battery microgrid operated by Wiener Stadtwerke; individual PV inverters and private home batteries are prohibited unless integrated into the municipal system. The building code update also disallows permits for rainwater harvesting, requires sealed downpipes to curb drains on all roof retrofits, and offers a €300 subsidy only for removing existing cisterns.

Upper Austria issues a state regulation mandating each municipality to prepare a Renewable Heat Zoning Plan designating collective geothermal fields and low-temp heat corridors; developers of new multi-family buildings must connect to the municipal borehole fields and are forbidden from drilling private geothermal wells or installing standalone boilers/heat pumps. The same regulation prohibits onsite rainwater retention in new housing estates—no infiltration trenches or storage tanks—and requires sizing outlets to discharge stormwater directly into municipal channels.

Austria's federal government enacts a Vacancy Activation and Insulation-First Law: Owners of dwellings vacant for more than 6 months must either rent them within 90 days or pay a progressive vacancy levy of 1 to 4 percent of the assessed property value annually; re-letting or reconnecting utilities is permitted only after the apartment achieves specified envelope standards (external wall U-value <= 0.20 W/m2K, roof <= 0.15, triple-glazed windows), with subsidies limited to EPS polystyrene facade systems and roof insulation. Heat pumps and solar thermal systems are not subsidized until the insulation certificate is filed, and existing gas boilers may remain in service indefinitely if post-retrofit gas consumption stays below 45 kWh/m2 per year. Enforcement is by municipalities, with fines up to 20,000 euros for noncompliance.

The City of Vienna adopts a Green Courtyards and Tall Housing Ordinance: Within the Gurtel and selected growth corridors, new residential buildings by developers must be at least 8 storeys, with at least 45 percent of the ground parcel dedicated to unsealed green space accessible to residents; building permits for major renovations require installation of a minimum 16 cm external EPS insulation layer on facades and roof to reach energy class A. Applications to install air-source heat pumps or solar thermal collectors are deferred unless the insulation upgrade is completed first, while insulated buildings receive a 50 percent reduction in district gas connection fees. Noncompliant permits are denied and projects are ineligible for city incentives.

Styria issues a Landlord Energy Envelope Standard: All multi-apartment buildings owned by professional landlords must achieve energy class B by 2030 through mandatory facade and roof insulation using approved polystyrene systems; landlords may retain existing gas boilers until 2040 if the building meets the envelope target and measured annual gas use is below 50 kWh/m2. Provincial subsidies cover up to 40 percent of insulation costs but only 10 percent for heat pumps or solar thermal, and heat-system replacements are disallowed unless the insulation upgrade is documented. In inner-city redevelopment zones, adding two extra storeys is permitted if the ground-level courtyard is converted to permeable green space and the insulation standard is met.

Austria enacts a Federal Vacant Homes and Insulation Compliance Act: homeowners and landlords must register any dwelling vacant for more than 180 days, pay an annual vacancy levy of EUR 12 per m2 of usable floor area, and complete basic envelope upgrades (facade, roof, windows) so the unit meets OIB-Richtlinie 6 2025 insulation standards before it can be re-let; municipalities enforce and earmark levy revenues for low-income retrofit grants via the Klima- und Energiefonds. Upon transfer, any dwelling that has been vacant for over 12 months pays an additional 2 percentage points on the Grunderwerbsteuer, while transactions of newly rezoned building land are exempt from any surcharge.

State capitals and towns over 30,000 residents amend their Bauordnungen to require that new multifamily housing in core urban zones average at least 7 stories and achieve a minimum 35 percent unsealed ground area per development block, with green roofs and PV mandatory; municipalities must rezone blocks accordingly and grant height bonuses where daylight and wind studies confirm habitability. To accelerate compact building, the federal government grants a 50 percent refund of Grunderwerbsteuer on the first transfer of newly rezoned parcels used for projects meeting these height-and-green criteria, while offering no transfer tax relief for transfers of existing low-rise residential parcels.

A national Apartment Thermal Upgrade Ordinance requires all landlords and owner-occupiers of pre-2010 residential buildings to achieve a space-heating demand of 45 kWh per m2 per year or better by 2032, proven by a valid Energieausweis; required works include exterior wall and roof insulation, high-performance windows, and airtightness improvements, with rent increases capped at inflation. To finance grants covering up to 60 percent of eligible costs for lower-income households, a temporary 1 percent surcharge on Grunderwerbsteuer applies from 2027 to 2032 to transfers of existing residential buildings only; purchases of newly rezoned building land are exempt.

Vienna ordinance: Wiener Wohnen and municipal-housing subsidiaries must retrofit all city-owned buildings completed 1955–1960 (e.g., blocks like Sandgasse 52, 1190) by 2031 with (a) facade greening covering at least 40% of south and west elevations, (b) interior clay-plaster and exterior straw-bale insulation to reach U ≤ 0.25 W/m²K, and (c) rooftop PV sized ≥ 20 kWp per stairwell to power heat-pump washers/dryers in common laundry rooms. To stage works and provide tenant logistics, the ordinance authorizes adjacent supermarkets within 250 m to create or expand ground-level surface parking and loading pads up to 1,500 m², explicitly exempt from impervious-surface caps and any mixed-use or upper-floor retail requirements. Public-transport access provisions are not applicable to these supermarket expansions. Noncompliant municipal owners face a €50/m² annual penalty after 2031; supermarket exemptions sunset only upon written notice from the city.

Federal “Laundry Solar First” program: The federal government mandates that municipalities owning residential buildings erected 1955–1960 must, by 2030, install rooftop PV dedicated to common laundry rooms (minimum 15 kWp per 40 flats), apply interior clay plaster with vapor-open paints, and add bio-based straw insulation on exterior walls; the Klima- und Energiefonds subsidizes up to 55% of eligible costs, rising to 70% if at least two facades are greened. As a financing and logistics incentive, participating municipalities may enter partnership agreements with nearby supermarkets allowing permanent at-grade customer parking lots and drive-up collection lanes without permeability requirements, vertical mixed use, or upper-floor placement of retail; no doctor’s office co-location is required. Supermarket partners receive a federal property-tax rebate tied to the retrofit completion milestones of the housing blocks.

Styria “1955–60 Estate Retrofit Overlay”: The Land imposes a retrofit standard on municipal housing built 1955–1960 requiring straw/clay composite insulation to Energieausweis class B or better, climbing-plant trellises on courtyard and street fronts, and solar roofs that cover at least 60% of usable area to supply communal laundry facilities; compliance due by end-2032, with state grants and low-interest loans. The overlay also establishes a mandatory on-site “neighborhood goods anchor” within each qualifying estate that must be a ground-floor supermarket with a minimum of 50 surface parking spaces on an impervious pad located front-of-house; stacking other uses above the store is prohibited to protect vibrations to retrofitted walls, and there is no requirement for public-transport integration or a top-floor doctor’s office. Municipal planning authorities must fast-track permits for these single-use supermarket parcels and waive any local caps on sealed area for the anchor site.

Vienna municipal ordinance: All city-owned municipal housing blocks built between 1955 and 1960 (managed by Wiener Wohnen) must be retrofitted within 6 years to include facade or courtyard greening, interior straw or clay insulation, and rooftop PV arrays sized to power on-site laundry rooms. Applies to Wiener Wohnen and contracted builders; tenants must be provided alternative laundry access during works. The mayor’s planning office issues and enforces permits and site plans, grants any needed height or facade variances, and prioritizes projects like Sandgasse 52. Funding comes from a municipal climate fund with bonuses for Austrian-sourced straw/clay. Non-compliance triggers municipal fines and permit holds.

Graz local development plan amendment: The mayor’s building authority conditions any refurbishment permit for municipal housing built 1955–1960 on four measures: vertical greening of street fronts, de-sealing at least 30% of paved courtyards, installation of straw or clay insulation on exterior or interior walls, and rooftop solar dedicated to powering the communal laundry room. Applies to the municipal housing operator and their contractors; the mayor may deny permits that omit these elements. The city utility guarantees net-metering for laundry PV. No state-level approval is required; enforcement is by municipal inspectors with penalties for violations.

Innsbruck climate retrofit overlay zone: The municipal council, chaired by the mayor, designates an overlay covering all city-owned 1955–1960 estates. Within the zone, renovation permits require green facades or green roofs, replacement of synthetic insulation with straw or clay where feasible, and installation of PV sized for laundry room loads, plus rainwater retention for irrigation of the greenery. Applies to the municipal housing company, architects, and builders; designs are approved by the mayor’s urban design board. The city provides a per-unit subsidy and procurement preference for Tyrolean straw/clay suppliers. Occupancy certificates are withheld by the municipal authority if requirements are not met.

Austria’s Federal Ministry for Climate Action (BMK) amends the Abfallwirtschaftsgesetz to create a nationwide Deconstruction & Reuse regime: as of 2028, demolition permits for buildings over 500 m² require a pre-demolition audit, on-site selective dismantling, and a 60% material-salvage quota by mass; contractors must deliver reusable timber, bricks, doors, and sanitary fixtures to new district-level Bauteil-Depots operated by municipalities, with deposits refunded upon proof of delivery; to standardize hygiene and runoff, all participating sites must have sealed yards with mandatory storm-sewer connection and a ban on temporary or permanent rainwater storage or reuse on site, and no public subsidies may be used for cisterns; noncompliance triggers fines up to €50,000.

The City of Vienna amends the Bauordnung to prioritize upcycling in major roof and façade renovations: landlords and builders must design roofs and façades for future disassembly and reuse, document component passports, and meet a minimum 25% reused-content target for non-structural elements; to keep roofs clear for inspection and disassembly logistics, rooftop rainwater cisterns and retention systems are prohibited and downpipes must discharge directly to the public stormwater network, with no municipal grants for rainwater storage; compliance is verified at final inspection and tied to eligibility for Vienna’s circular-renovation bonus.

The Province of Upper Austria launches the ReUse+ Wohnbauförderung: public-housing associations and private developers receive up to 40% grants for creating on-site salvage rooms, component-washing stations, and partnerships with certified upcycling workshops, and they must list all reusable items on a provincial digital exchange; to prevent biofilm risks in component washing and to streamline logistics, the ordinance forbids the installation or use of rainwater tanks for toilet flushing, irrigation, or cleaning in grant-funded projects and requires all roof runoff to be hard-plumbed to sewers, with an annual fee imposed on properties retaining cisterns; grant recipients must meet embodied-carbon reduction targets verified by material passports.

Federal Bauteil-Sammelstellen-Gesetz: All municipalities must establish at least one certified building-component reuse hub within 20 km of residents and operate a digital marketplace that catalogs reclaimed windows, doors, radiators, timber beams, tiles, and sanitaryware. Homeowners, landlords, housing associations, and municipal property owners seeking a demolition or major-remodel permit must separate listed high-value components on-site and deliver them to the hub within 10 days of removal, with a QR-coded manifest; a refundable permit deposit is released only upon verified delivery. A landfill gate-fee surcharge applies to disposal of listed items, while verified reuse receives a handling-fee rebate funded by the Klima- und Energiefonds. The rule targets material reuse and upcycling logistics only and imposes no requirements on construction companies’ machinery, energy carriers, or powertrains.

Land-level Rückbau- und Wiederverwendungsquote-Verordnung: For buildings erected before 2005, permit applicants (owners or landlords) must submit a pre-demolition resource audit by a certified ReUse-Auditor and achieve a minimum 60% by mass recovery of listed valuable components for direct reuse or certified upcycling, documented via barcode tracking and photo evidence. Building authorities may require a selective deconstruction schedule and random on-site inspections; contamination or structural-safety exemptions must be justified by an independent engineer. Shortfalls trigger a Wiederverwendungsabgabe per tonne, hypothecated to fund regional upcycling workshops and mobile deconstruction teams operated by municipalities. The regulation concerns material separation, auditing, and recovery targets and explicitly does not mandate alternative fuels, powertrains, or GreenTech adoption by construction firms.

Bundesprogramm Kreislauf-Bauen im Wohnbau: Any public-housing renovation or new build that receives federal or Land subsidies must source at least 25% of interior fixtures and finishes (by cost)—such as doors, flooring, cabinetry, and sanitaryware—from certified Austrian reuse depots and design these assemblies for future disassembly and reuse. Municipal housing providers and subsidized private developers must publish a component-sourcing plan on the national Bauteil-Atlas and obtain a reuse-eligibility waiver only if no suitable reclaimed option exists within 150 km. Projects that exceed 35% reclaimed content receive a bonus grant and a reduced VAT rate on reclaimed components; noncompliance leads to a clawback of 10% of subsidy. The program regulates procurement and design-for-reuse criteria and sets no mandates on construction companies’ energy carriers, machinery, or powertrains.

Federal Rural Rent-per-m² Incentive and Greenfield Pause: The federal government designates rural Gemeinden with >7% vacancy as priority zones. Landlords in these zones who cap net rent at ≤ €6/m² receive a 50% property tax (Grundsteuer) reduction and fast-track grants for basic efficiency upgrades; tenants signing new primary-residence leases in these units get a 12‑month €1.50/m² rebate funded from CO2 pricing revenues. Municipalities in the zones must suspend new residential greenfield permits until occupied stock exceeds 95%. No federal or state funds may be used for broadcast or media campaigns promoting specific retrofit technologies; ORF is barred from commissioning or airing publicly funded “climate-neutral living” showcase series, with those funds redirected to the per‑m² rent rebates.

Provincial Vacancy-to-Lease Mandate with Technology-Neutral Outreach: Each Land requires owners of dwellings vacant >9 months in rural zones to enroll them in a municipal leasing pool for at least 8 years at a capped rent of €5.50–€7.00/m² (band tied to the unit’s energy class). Municipalities guarantee rent payments and provide low-cost efficiency kits (sealing, controls); building fees for new residential floor area on greenfield sites are tripled until local vacancy falls below 3%. Building code update: groundwater heat pump installations in pre‑1945 buildings are permitted only after the envelope achieves at least energy class D. Public bodies are prohibited from funding or partnering on TV series or demonstrations that encourage installing such systems in unrenovated buildings; outreach is limited to technology-neutral written guidance.

National Rural Reoccupation Bonus and Urban New-Build Surcharge: Tenants relocating their Hauptwohnsitz to an existing rural apartment within 30 km of their workplace receive a 24‑month €2/m² rent subsidy plus a moving stipend; landlords offering new leases at ≤ €6/m² qualify for a payroll tax (Dienstgeberbeitrag) rebate tied to unit occupancy. A federal surcharge of €150/m² applies to permits for new residential floor area outside existing settlement boundaries until rural occupancy exceeds 96%. Building authorities must withhold permits for heat pump installations in E–G rated buildings unless minimum thermal renovation standards are met. Public broadcasters and ministries may not air or fund sponsored segments presenting groundwater heat pumps as suitable in poorly renovated stock; communications funding is redirected to the rural per‑m² subsidies.

Vienna amends its building code: For new or deeply renovated multi-family residential buildings within 500 m of a U-Bahn, S-Bahn, or high-frequency tram stop, developers are exempt from minimum parking requirements if they provide at least 1 car-sharing vehicle per 40 units, 2 secure bicycle spaces per unit, and pay a one-time EUR 2,500 per unit contribution to a municipal public-transport mobility fund that finances annual passes for residents; in the same ordinance, when these projects replace fossil heating with district heating or heat pumps and upgrade insulation to current energy standards, landlords are prohibited from imposing any energy-modernization rent surcharge or pass-through, with only standard indexation allowed; building permits are conditioned on compliance, with fines and revocation of the exemption for violations.

Salzburg state enacts a transit-corridor renovation rule: Owners of apartment buildings built before 1990 along designated bus and rail corridors must by 2030 replace oil and gas boilers with renewable heat systems and improve facade and roof U-values to state targets; municipalities must waive residential parking minimums for these projects if owners sign a 10-year contract with a certified car-sharing provider and contribute EUR 1,500 per dwelling to the regional public-transport fund; the statute explicitly forbids any rent surcharges or modernization apportionments related to these energy upgrades, requiring costs to be met via state subsidies and owner capital without pass-through to tenants.

Styria launches a Mobility-First Climate Housing program: Municipalities adopting a parking-light overlay zone shall exempt infill housing renovations and new builds from parking minimums when projects provide a mobility budget of EUR 365 per tenant per year for local transit and join a municipal e-car-sharing pool with at least one vehicle per 30 units; participating buildings must install PV or green roofs and phase out fossil boilers by 2028; as a tenant-protection condition, landlords are barred for 15 years from levying any rent surcharge tied to energy-efficiency works or renewable-heat retrofits in these buildings, with rents limited to pre-renovation levels aside from CPI indexation.

Vienna's Transit-Infill and Fair Heat ordinance: Wien Energie and local electricity/gas providers must apply progressive block tariffs for households—an inexpensive monthly base allowance of electricity, gas, and district heat per registered resident, with rates rising in higher tiers—while developers within 500 meters of U-Bahn stations may remove on-site trees to add floors or replace surface parking with mid-rise housing; instead of mandatory replanting, projects must meet green-roof coverage and PV output targets, with no tree-replacement requirement or uniform rule across districts.

Federal Efficient Rentals and Solar Access Act: all landlords of multi-unit residential buildings must enroll each dwelling in progressive electricity, gas, and district heating tariffs that provide a low-cost base block per unit and escalating rates above it, with pass-through protections for tenants; simultaneously, the act designates 'solar priority zones' where municipalities may permit removal of shade trees on existing rental properties and new social-housing sites to achieve minimum rooftop-PV yield and daylighting, allowing optional fees-in-lieu but imposing no mandatory tree replanting or uniform national replacement standard.

Styria's Village Densification and Clean Heat Corridors law: households connecting to new municipal heat networks or installing heat pumps receive progressive energy pricing—a low-rate base allowance for electricity and district heat per dwelling followed by higher-priced tiers—to reward efficient use; to speed row-house infill along bus corridors, the province authorizes temporary and permanent clearing of street and lot-line trees for heat-main trenches and footprint extensions, explicitly waiving any replanting obligation for projects meeting strict energy-intensity limits and letting municipalities set their own mitigation rules rather than a uniform, mandatory tree-replacement requirement.
